definition: The Cambridge Language Research Unit (CLRU) was founded by Margaret Masterman in 1954 to bring together researches from different academic backgrounds to study the possibility of machine translation.
details: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology publication Machine Translation published a special issue in 1956 dedicated to the CLRU noting that mechanical translation was, at that time an area of study unexplored within the official curriculum of any English university. Based in Millington Road, Cambridge the unit picked up on the conjectural role of an intermediate language with antecedents in the seventeenth century work of John Wilkins and George Dalgarno.

explainer.lead: The Cambridge Language Research Unit was an interdisciplinary group founded by Margaret Masterman in Cambridge in 1954 to investigate machine translation. It explored whether an intermediate language could carry meaning between languages, an idea with roots in seventeenth-century scholarship.

tiers.eli5: The unit brought together people with different kinds of knowledge to ask whether computers could translate languages. One idea was like using a shared secret code: turn a sentence into that code first, then turn the code into another language.
tiers.practitioner: CLRU is a historical research organization, not a translation tool or software library. Its interlingua line of inquiry corresponds to the engineering pattern source text -> intermediate meaning representation -> target text, but no specific implementation or tools are documented.
tiers.paperLevel: CLRU was founded in 1954 to study machine translation across academic disciplines. Its research considered an intermediate language as a conjectural bridge between source and target languages, with antecedents in the seventeenth-century work of John Wilkins and George Dalgarno.
